chapter_summary:
Having mastered the basics, we now dive into the more sophisticated post-processing effects that can truly elevate your scene's realism and cinematic quality. These effects often simulate complex optical phenomena or global illumination, demanding more computational resources but delivering stunning visual fidelity. As a 3D artist, understanding their purpose and how to balance visual impact with performance is key.

One of the most visually striking effects is **Depth of Field (DoF)**. This effect simulates the optical properties of a camera lens, where objects at a certain distance are in sharp focus, while objects closer or further away appear blurred. DoF is incredibly powerful for directing the viewer's eye, creating a sense of scale, or achieving a cinematic, photographic look. You'll typically adjust `Focus Distance` (the distance from the camera where objects are perfectly sharp), `Aperture` (controlling the strength of the blur and the size of bokeh highlights), and `Focal Length`. A common mistake is applying too much blur, making the scene look artificial or disorienting. Use DoF subtly to enhance focus rather than obscure details.

**Screen Space Reflections (SSR)** is another high-impact effect that simulates reflections on shiny surfaces. Unlike traditional reflection probes which capture reflections from a single point, SSR calculates reflections based on what's currently visible on the screen. This allows for dynamic, real-time reflections on surfaces like wet floors, polished metals, or water puddles. You'll configure `Max Roughness` (how rough a surface can be to still show reflections), `Resolution`, and `Intensity`. While visually impressive, SSR is one of the most performance-intensive post-processing effects. It's calculated in screen space, meaning it can only reflect what the camera can see, and it can introduce visual artifacts if not carefully tuned. A safety note here is to use SSR judiciously and at lower `Resolution` settings for performance-critical applications.

**Screen Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO)** is an effect that approximates the darkening of surfaces where ambient light is occluded, such as in crevices, corners, or under objects. It adds a subtle but significant sense of depth and realism by simulating soft shadows in areas that would naturally receive less ambient light. You'll adjust `Intensity`, `Radius` (how far the occlusion spreads), and `Thickness Modifier`. SSAO is less computationally expensive than SSR but still contributes to the overall render budget. It's excellent for grounding objects in a scene and making them feel less "floating."

Other advanced effects include **Chromatic Aberration** (simulating lens distortion where colors separate at the edges of objects), **Grain** (adding a film-like noise texture), and **Lens Distortion** (simulating barrel or pincushion distortion of a camera lens). These effects can add character and realism, especially when aiming for a specific camera aesthetic.

Beyond individual effects, understanding **Post-Process Volumes** and their blending capabilities is crucial for dynamic scene transitions. You can have multiple volumes in a scene, each with its own profile and effects. If `Is Global` is unchecked, a volume acts as a trigger zone. As your camera moves between these volumes, Unity can smoothly blend the post-processing effects, allowing for seamless transitions between different moods or visual styles. For example, entering a dark cave might trigger a volume with increased `Vignette` and a cooler `Color Grading`, while exiting into a bright forest could blend back to a vibrant, warm profile. This blending is controlled by the `Blend Distance` property on the local volume. This powerful feature allows artists to craft immersive and responsive visual experiences that react to player progression or environmental changes. Always remember to profile your scene when adding multiple complex effects to ensure you maintain target frame rates.

screens.title: Advanced Post-Processing Effects & Customization
screens.subtitle: Depth of Field, SSR, SSAO and blending multiple post-process volumes to shape mood and realism

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will learn how advanced post-processing effects elevate realism and cinematic mood in a scene while also learning to keep an eye on performance. We define each effect, show the primary parameters you will tune, and provide concrete settings and a short hands-on workflow you can follow in your scene. For example, Depth of Field lets you emphasize a subject by choosing a focus distance and aperture; Screen Space Reflections deliver dynamic reflections based on what the camera sees, but they cost G P U time and can show artifacts; Screen Space Ambient Occlusion adds subtle shadowing in crevices to ground objects. You will also learn how to use multiple post-process volumes to create environmental transitions, such as entering a cave that becomes colder and more vignetted as you cross a blend distance. Throughout the module we highlight common mistakes — like over-blurring with DoF or running SSR at full resolution — and show practical trade-offs. By the end you will be able to pick and tune effects to match an artistic mood while staying performance-aware.

narration.text: In this chapter you will gain concrete skills for implementing and tuning advanced post-processing effects. First, you will learn to add and configure Depth of Field, and adjust Focus Distance and Aperture to direct viewer attention. Second, you will enable Screen Space Reflections and balance Max Roughness, Intensity, and Resolution to capture dynamic reflections without overwhelming performance. Each objective includes why the skill matters and a short mental model to help you remember the setting trade-offs. For example, think of aperture like a camera iris: lower values produce stronger blur and larger bokeh, which can be striking but easy to overuse. Finally, you will use Post-Process Volumes and blending to create local mood shifts. This set of objectives focuses on the practical actions and the artistic reasoning you need to make choices that support both visual fidelity and playability.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Deeper view
screens.subtitle: Practical skills, mnemonics, and performance-aware decisions

narration.text: This second objectives slide gives you the practical heuristics and mnemonics to retain the settings. Remember: aperture is the strength of blur and should be treated like an iris — lower values create stronger blur and larger bokeh. For reflections, think of SSR as a local mirror that only reflects what the camera can see; when you need global reflections use static probes, but for dynamic moving objects SSR is appropriate with reduced resolution. For ambient occlusion, imagine tiny soft shadows that appear in crevices; increase radius to grow the occlusion footprint, and raise intensity to make it visible, but avoid heavy values that make the scene look dirty or crushed. Finally, for blending volumes, use a meaningful blend distance to hide abrupt visual jumps. These heuristics help you pick initial values that you can iterate on in play mode while profiling performance and checking for visual artifacts.

keyIdea.title: Heuristics
keyIdea.text: Use camera metaphors and simple heuristics: aperture for blur, SSR as camera-limited reflections, SSAO for crevice shadowing, and Blend Distance for smooth transitions.

Practical mnemonics
Quick mental models and trade-offs to speed decision-making during iteration.
Aperture = Iris
Treat aperture like a camera iris. Start with conservative values and lower aperture only when you want strong cinematic separation. Too much blur hides important detail.

SSR = Screen mirror

Use SSAO to ground objects. Increase radius for broader contact shadows and intensity to make them visible, but avoid crushing the midtones.
Visual mnemonic: corner shadow

screens.title: Depth of Field (DoF) — definition and purpose
screens.subtitle: Simulating camera focus to direct attention and create scale

narration.text: Depth of Field simulates how a camera lens renders focus: objects at a specific focus distance remain sharp while nearer or farther elements appear blurred. This creates a photographic look and helps direct the viewer's attention to a subject. In practice you set a Focus Distance to define the plane of perfect sharpness, an Aperture to control the blur strength and bokeh characteristics, and sometimes a Focal Length to influence perceived compression. A concrete example: a character close to the camera with a focus distance set to their eyes will appear crisp while the background foliage blurs, emphasizing emotion without changing the geometry. A common misconception is that bigger blur is always better; too much blur can hide important gameplay cues or make navigation harder. Instead, treat DoF as a compositional tool: start subtle, iterate in play mode, and verify that interactive elements remain readable. As a quick test, toggle DoF on and off to judge whether the compositional improvement outweighs any loss of clarity. Depth of Field (DoF) — definition and purpose means dof uses focus distance and aperture to simulate lens focus and guide the viewer's eye while preserving readable detail.. In practical terms, simulating camera focus to direct attention and create scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Tuning Depth of Field — practical steps
screens.subtitle: How to choose Focus Distance and Aperture for real scenes

narration.text: Tuning Depth of Field is an iterative process. Start in play mode and identify your visual subject. First, set Focus Distance to that subject so it sits on the plane of sharpness. Second, reduce Aperture gradually to introduce blur; observe foreground and background elements to ensure no critical detail is lost. Third, tweak Focal Length if you need a more compressed or telephoto feel. A concrete workflow: set Focus Distance to the player's head in a character close-up, then set Aperture to a conservative value like five or six and lower it only if the background separation is still insufficient. Check the scene at several camera positions and movement speeds to make sure the blur does not cause motion sickness or hide UI. A misconception is assuming a single DoF value works everywhere; instead use local Post-Process Volumes or dynamic scripts to change settings for special shots. Finally, test on target hardware and toggle DoF to ensure the aesthetic gains justify the performance cost. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Tuning Depth of Field
Process
  1. Identify the subject and set Focus Distance to its depth.
  2. Reduce Aperture incrementally to introduce subtle blur.
  3. Tweak Focal Length for compression if desired.
  4. Validate across camera positions and motion speeds.
  5. Use local volumes for scene-specific DoF changes.
Key Takeaway

Iterative checks in play mode are essential; subtle DoF often reads better than strong blur.

Concrete example
For a 3rd-person character close-up, set Focus Distance to the head at 2–5 units and set Aperture to a conservative value, then reduce until the background separation reads without obscuring the hands or UI.
Pitfall
Assuming a single DoF profile fits all cameras; instead use local volumes or camera-specific profiles for dramatic shots.
Try toggling DoF in play mode to compare readability and cinematic effect. Start subtle, then push only where the scene benefits; always confirm the result on your target hardware.

screens.title: Screen Space Reflections (SSR) — purpose and limits
screens.subtitle: Dynamic, camera-based reflections and their screen-space constraints

narration.text: Screen Space Reflections create real-time reflections by sampling what the camera currently renders. They are excellent for shiny floors, water puddles, and polished surfaces because they can reflect dynamic objects without baking. However, SSR only knows about what is visible on-screen, so it cannot reflect off-screen elements and can produce artifacts where geometry lies outside the camera view or where rough surfaces obstruct rays. Typical parameters you'll touch are Max Roughness which limits how rough a surface can be and still show reflections, Resolution which dictates the internal buffer quality, and Intensity which scales reflection contribution. A common practical trade-off is to set Resolution to Half or Quarter to save performance while retaining believable reflections. Use SSR for dynamic surfaces where probes are insufficient, but fall back to reflection probes or screen-space blending when you need consistent global reflections. Test reflections across camera angles to spot missing or stretched artifacts and adjust Max Roughness and Resolution accordingly. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Screen Space Reflections
Core Concept
Screen Space Reflections
Real-time reflections calculated from pixels already rendered to the screen.
Strengths
Dynamic reflections for moving objects and specular surfaces without baking.
Limits
Only reflects what appears on-screen; off-screen geometry and occluded rays create artifacts.
Key Takeaway

Use SSR for dynamic, on-screen reflections and combine with probes for coverage where SSR cannot reach.

Tunable parameters
Max Roughness
Defines how rough a surface can be and still show SSR reflections.
Resolution
Internal buffer quality. Half or Quarter reduce cost with softer results.
Intensity
Scales reflection contribution to the final shaded result.

screens.title: SSR performance trade-offs and tuning
screens.subtitle: Balancing reflection quality and render cost

narration.text: SSR can be visually striking but expensive. The primary lever you have is Resolution: Full resolution yields crisp reflections but is costly; Half or Quarter resolution reduces G P U workload and introduces softness that is often acceptable on moving reflective surfaces. Max Roughness controls which surfaces can show SSR. Lowering Max Roughness limits reflections to very smooth surfaces and reduces work done when many rough surfaces would otherwise be sampled. Intensity scales how much SSR contributes; lowering it can hide artifacts while keeping the impression of reflection. A concrete trade-off example: on consoles, set Resolution to Half and lower Max Roughness to 0.8 to permit reflections only on relatively smooth materials, then reduce Intensity to 0.5 to avoid visual noise. A common misconception is that SSR must replace probes; it should supplement them. Use SSR for dynamic elements and probes for global, off-screen or distant reflections. Always profile after changes to confirm frame-rate gains. SSR performance trade-offs and tuning means reduce resolution and constrain roughness to keep reflections believable without excessive cost; combine ssr with probes for coverage.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SSR tuning
keyIdea.text: Reduce resolution and constrain roughness to keep reflections believable without excessive cost; combine SSR with probes for coverage.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › SSR: Performance trade-offs
Options and effect
Resolution
Lower to save performance; expect softer, blurrier reflections.
Max Roughness
Limit reflections to smoother surfaces to reduce sampling work.
Intensity
Lower to blend reflections more subtly and mask artifacts.
Concrete tuning example
Recommended trade-off

Set SSR Resolution to Half, Max Roughness to ~0.8, and Intensity to 0.5 on constrained hardware to keep reflections believable while lowering cost.

Misconception
Expecting SSR to cover every reflective need. In practice combine SSR with reflection probes for off-screen and distant reflections.

screens.title: Screen Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO)
screens.subtitle: Approximating soft contact shadows to ground objects

narration.text: Screen Space Ambient Occlusion approximates the soft darkening that occurs where ambient light is occluded, for example in crevices, corners, or under overhangs. It is not a replacement for full global illumination but a cost-effective technique to increase perceived depth. The primary parameters to tune are Intensity, which scales how dark the occlusion appears; Radius, which controls how far away samples contribute to the occlusion; and Thickness Modifier, which adjusts sensitivity to thin geometry. A practical example: enabling SSAO at moderate intensity with a radius of around 0.5 creates subtle darkening under furniture and in gaps, making objects appear more weighted. A misconception is that very high intensity always improves realism; instead, excessive SSAO can make a scene look dirty or crushed. Use SSAO modestly to enhance contact shadows and combine it with careful light setup and proper material profiles to achieve natural results. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Screen Space Ambient Occlusion
Definition
Approximate soft shadows where ambient light is occluded to enhance depth perception in a scene.
Intensity
Controls darkness of occlusion.
Radius
How far occlusion spreads from geometry.
Thickness Modifier
Adjusts sensitivity to thin features.
Concrete example
Enable SSAO with Intensity 1.0 and Radius 0.5 to add subtle shadows in gaps beneath objects and along corners. This helps the scene feel grounded without fully darkening midtones.
Key Takeaway

SSAO is a lightweight depth cue. Keep it subtle to avoid a dirty or crushed look.

Common mistake
Using high intensity or radius values that create unrealistic darkening around objects and reduce material clarity.

screens.title: Adding DoF, SSR, and SSAO to a Post-Process Profile
screens.subtitle: Hands-on workflow from the chapter activity

narration.text: Follow a simple sequence to add these effects to your Post-Process Profile. Start with your existing profile and open the Post-Process Volume component. Add Depth of Field, enable overrides for Mode and Focus Distance, and set Mode to Gaussian for predictable blur. Choose a Focus Distance that targets your subject and set Aperture conservatively, as discussed. Next add Screen Space Reflections, enable Intensity override and set it to about 0.5, then set Max Roughness to around 0.8 and Resolution to Half to balance quality and cost. Finally, add Screen Space Ambient Occlusion and set Intensity to 1.0 and Radius to 0.5 as a starting point. Play the scene and observe how each change affects the look: move the camera and check for SSR artifacts, check whether DoF hides interactive elements, and ensure SSAO does not overly darken important surfaces. The chapter activity suggests creating a second local volume to practice blending; we'll cover how to set that up next. Always iterate while profiling to confirm that visual benefits justify G P U expense. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Add DoF, SSR, SSAO
Follow these steps in your Post-Process Profile and validate in play mode.
1. Add Depth of Field
  • Click Add Effect > Unity > Depth Of Field.
  • Override Mode to Gaussian and set Focus Distance to subject.
  • Set Aperture conservatively and test in play mode.
2. Add Screen Space Reflections
  • Add Screen Space Reflections and enable Intensity override at 0.5.
  • Set Max Roughness to around 0.8 and Resolution to Half for performance.
3. Add SSAO
  • Add Screen Space Ambient Occlusion and set Intensity to 1.0.
  • Start with Radius 0.5 and adjust Thickness Modifier for thin features.
Check your result
Play the scene, look for SSR artifacts, verify that DoF does not obscure UI or gameplay, and ensure SSAO adds depth without crushing midtones. If performance drops, reduce SSR resolution or lower DoF precision.

screens.title: Create and blend a local Post-Process Volume
screens.subtitle: Using un-checked Is Global volumes and Blend Distance for mood shifts

narration.text: Blending multiple Post-Process Volumes lets you change visual mood based on location. Create a second Post-Process Volume with Is Global unchecked to make it local. Place it in the world where you want the mood change — for instance, inside a cave. Assign a new profile that increases Vignette and shifts Color Grading toward cooler tones to suggest darkness. Set a Blend Distance on the local volume to create a soft transition area around the volume bounds. When the camera crosses into the blend region Unity interpolates between the active global profile and the local profile over that distance, producing a smooth visual shift. A concrete scenario: outside forest lighting is vibrant, then entering the cave gradually increases vignette and desaturates color as you cross the blend boundary. A common error is using a zero blend distance, which causes abrupt jumps. Always tune blend distances to camera movement speed and test transitions in play mode to ensure they feel natural. Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Post-Process Volumes
Create local volume
Uncheck Is Global to make a volume that only affects the camera inside its bounds. Assign a dedicated profile and set Blend Distance to soften the transition.
Example profile
Increase Vignette, lower Color Grading saturation, and slightly darken exposure for cave mood.
Pitfall
A zero Blend Distance makes abrupt visual jumps; always use a blend buffer sized to camera speed.
Concrete scenario
Place a local volume at a cave entrance. Set Blend Distance so that moving into the cave the vignette and desaturation build gradually over a few meters, avoiding sudden changes that break immersion.
Key Takeaway

Blend Distance is the control that makes local volumes feel natural. Tune it against camera motion and spatial scale.

screens.title: Chromatic Aberration, Grain, and Lens Distortion
screens.subtitle: Subtle lens effects for character and film grain

narration.text: Beyond the physically based effects, small camera lens treatments add character and mood. Chromatic Aberration simulates color separation near image edges, suggesting imperfect lenses or dramatic distortion; use it sparingly to avoid visual discomfort. Grain adds a film-like noise texture that can unify a frame and hide banding, but excessive grain reduces clarity and can conflict with UI legibility. Lens Distortion simulates barrel or pincushion distortion and can be useful for stylized camera feels or to mimic wide-angle optics. A practical approach is to use these effects at low intensities as finishing touches: apply a subtle grain layer to unify tone, a small amount of chromatic aberration for stylization, and mild lens distortion only when you intend a stylistic quote of camera optics. A common mistake is using these effects to hide poor art or lighting; instead, they should enhance an already good base render. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Simulates color fringing near image edges. Use low intensity for stylistic flair only.
Grain

Lens Distortion

screens.title: Observe, profile, and iterate
screens.subtitle: Validate visuals across camera positions and target hardware

narration.text: Adding advanced effects is only half the work. The other half is validation and iteration. After making changes, play the scene across the range of camera positions your application uses. Watch for DoF obscuring important readouts, SSR failing to reflect relevant objects from certain angles, or SSAO crushing midtones in shadowed areas. Run a performance profile on target hardware to find bottlenecks introduced by SSR resolution, DoF sample counts, or SSAO radius. If a single effect costs too much, use a combination of lower-cost approximations: reduce SSR resolution, lower DoF precision or enable DoF only for cinematic cameras, and reduce SSAO intensity. A practical check is to toggle each effect on and off in play mode and measure frame-time delta. Document the changes you make and their performance impact so you can make informed trade-offs later. The core idea is that aesthetic choices must be justified by testing and profiling. Observe, profile, and iterate means always validate effects across cameras and profile on target hardware; use toggles and measurements to justify visual decisions.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Key Takeaway

Make decisions with both visual checks and performance data. Iteration and profiling ensure the effects support gameplay and hardware targets.

screens.title: Common mistakes and pro tips
screens.subtitle: Avoid overuse, and use the right tool for the job

narration.text: There are recurring mistakes artists make when applying advanced post-processing. One is over-reliance on effects to fix lighting or composition problems. Effects should enhance, not conceal. Another is running SSR at full resolution by default; this often causes disproportionate performance cost compared with its visual gain. Similarly, applying very strong SSAO or DoF can make scenes look artificial or hide interactive elements. Pro tips from the chapter: use conservative default values, enable expensive effects only for cameras that need them, and mix SSR with static probes so you get dynamic reflections where needed and baked stability elsewhere. When creating local volumes, plan blend distances according to camera speed to avoid sharp transitions. Finally, always profile after changes and keep a documented set of presets for different hardware targets so you can toggle between high-quality and performance modes quickly. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Common mistakes & Pro tips
Common mistakes
  • Using post-processing to hide poor lighting or composition.
  • Running SSR at full resolution without profiling cost.
  • Applying extreme SSAO or DoF that reduces clarity or reads as dirty.
Pro tips
  • Use conservative defaults and enable expensive effects per-camera.
  • Combine SSR for dynamic objects with reflection probes for global coverage.
  • Create presets for different hardware targets to quickly adjust quality vs performance.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize readability and performance. Use post-processing to enhance, not to mask deeper issues.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Visual Effects
screens.subtitle: Three essential effects and why they matter

narration.text: Let's summarize three core visual effects. Depth of Field simulates lens focus; use Focus Distance to place the sharp plane and Aperture to control blur strength. It is invaluable for directing attention but should be used subtly so it does not hide gameplay elements. Screen Space Reflections calculate reflections from what's visible on screen; they are great for dynamic, polished surfaces but are limited to on-screen content and can be costly, so use lower resolutions as a performance trade-off. Screen Space Ambient Occlusion adds soft contact shadows in crevices to ground objects and improve depth perception; tune Intensity and Radius carefully to avoid a dirty look. These three effects together significantly affect perceived realism, but they must be balanced against performance and clarity. When in doubt, test toggles and profile changes to confirm whether an effect's aesthetic benefit justifies its cost.

keyIdea.title: Remember
keyIdea.text: Depth of Field, SSR, and SSAO are powerful when tuned together; keep effects subtle and validated on target hardware.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Key Concepts — Visual Effects
Depth of Field
Simulates camera focus; use Focus Distance and Aperture to control sharpness and blur.
Screen Space Reflections
Real-time reflections from screen pixels; limited to on-screen content and sensitive to resolution.
SSAO
Approximates ambient occlusion in crevices and corners to add soft contact shadows.
Summary takeaway
Combine these effects thoughtfully. Tune parameters conservatively, validate across camera movement, and profile on target hardware to balance fidelity and performance.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Volumes, Lens Effects, Performance
screens.subtitle: Three operational reminders before you finish

narration.text: Before you finish, remember three operational points. First, Local Post-Process Volumes let you change visual profiles in space; uncheck Is Global, assign a new profile, and set Blend Distance to interpolate. Second, Lens-based effects like Chromatic Aberration, Grain, and Lens Distortion are finishing touches. Use them at low intensity to add character without reducing clarity. Third, always profile performance impacts. Common high-cost culprits include SSR at full resolution and aggressive DoF sampling. The best workflow is to make conservative initial choices, test in play mode across camera motion, and measure frame-time deltas. If a setting is visually pleasing but too costly, lower resolution, reduce intensity, or restrict the effect to cinematic cameras or local volumes. These operational checks will keep your scenes both beautiful and playable. Local Volumes
Use unchecked Is Global volumes with Blend Distance to create spatial mood changes.
Lens Effects
Chromatic aberration, grain, and distortion should be low-intensity finishing touches.

Profile changes should be profiled. Lower SSR resolution and DoF precision when necessary.
Final takeaway
Balance artistry and performance: subtlety, profiling, and smart blending are what make advanced post-processing truly effective.
